content.title: Interpreting Range, IQR, and Standard Deviation
content.overview: This lesson focuses on measures of spread (variability) in univariate data. You will learn to distinguish between range, interquartile range (IQR), and standard deviation (SD), specifically how they are calculated and how they respond to extreme values or outliers.
learning_objectives: Calculate the range and interquartile range (IQR) from a data set or five-number summary.
Identify which measure of spread is most appropriate for a given statistical goal.
Predict how outliers affect range, IQR, and standard deviation.

sections.title: Measures of Spread Defined
sections.content: Measures of spread describe how 'stretched' or 'squeezed' a data set is. The Range is the simplest measure, calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum values (Range = Max - Min). The Interquartile Range (IQR) measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data, calculated as the difference between the third quartile and the first quartile (IQR = Q3 - Q1). Standard Deviation (SD) represents the typical or average distance of data points from the mean.

sections.title: Sensitivity to Outliers
sections.content: A critical concept for the ACT is how these measures react to outliers (extreme values). The Range is highly sensitive to outliers because it only uses the two most extreme points. Standard Deviation is also sensitive to outliers because every data point, including extremes, is used in its calculation; an outlier far from the mean will significantly increase the SD. In contrast, the IQR is 'robust' or resistant to outliers because it only considers the middle 50% of the data, effectively ignoring the tails of the distribution.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Measure
sections.content:
Use the Range when you need to know the total span of the data. Use the IQR when you want to describe the spread of the 'typical' data while ignoring extreme values or skewed tails. Use Standard Deviation when you need a measure that accounts for the position of every single data point relative to the average.

![A flowchart showing how to choose between Range, IQR, and Standard Deviation based on the presence of outliers.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/7d9ebe41-1fad-4501-8792-08a6d6371d21-1786506112667-368.webp)

worked_examples.question: A data set has a five-number summary of: Min=5, Q1=15, Median=20, Q3=30, Max=100. Calculate the Range and the IQR. Which measure better represents the spread of the majority of the data?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Calculate Range using Max - Min. Range = 100 - 5 = 95. Step 2: Calculate IQR using Q3 - Q1. IQR = 30 - 15 = 15. Step 3: Compare the results. The Range (95) is heavily influenced by the outlier (100). The IQR (15) describes the middle 50% of the data. Therefore, the IQR better represents the spread of the majority of the data by ignoring the extreme maximum.

common_mistakes: Confusing IQR with the range of the entire data set.
Assuming Standard Deviation is unaffected by outliers; it actually increases significantly when outliers are present.
Calculating IQR as Q3 - Q1 but forgetting that these values represent the 75th and 25th percentiles, not the max and min.
exam_tips: If an ACT question asks for a measure of spread that 'ignores extremes,' look for IQR in the answer choices.
Range and Standard Deviation always increase if you add a value further away from the mean than existing values.
You do not need to calculate Standard Deviation by hand on the ACT; you only need to understand what it represents conceptually.
content.recap: Range (Max-Min) and Standard Deviation are sensitive to outliers and describe total or typical spread. The IQR (Q3-Q1) focuses on the middle 50% and is the best measure for ignoring extreme values.

knowledge_claims.content: The range of a data set is calculated by subtracting the minimum value from the maximum value (Range = Max - Min).
The interquartile range (IQR) is calculated by subtracting the first quartile from the third quartile (IQR = Q3 - Q1).
Standard deviation represents the typical or average distance of data points from the mean of the data set.
The range is highly sensitive to outliers because it depends entirely on the most extreme values in the data set.
The interquartile range (IQR) is resistant to outliers because it only measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
Standard deviation increases when outliers are added to a data set because those points are far from the mean.
If a statistical question requires ignoring extreme values when describing spread, the interquartile range (IQR) is the appropriate measure.
The interquartile range (IQR) specifically describes the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution.
To find the IQR from a five-number summary, identify Q1 and Q3 and calculate their difference.
It is a mistake to assume that standard deviation is a robust measure; it is actually sensitive to extreme values.
Adding a new maximum value that is much higher than the previous maximum will increase both the range and the standard deviation.
To verify if a measure of spread is the range, check if it uses the difference between the absolute highest and lowest points.
